headline: OpenAI’s Head of Safety Johannes Heidecke Is Leaving Amidst Safety Team Reorganization
summary: Johannes Heidecke's departure follows a reorganization integrating OpenAI's safety and research teams. This comes as the company trains models faster and faces increased coordination challenges around safety.
details: OpenAI's head of safety systems, Johannes Heidecke, has informed staff of his departure. This move follows a significant reorganization aimed at integrating the company's safety and research teams more closely.

Chief Research Officer Mark Chen stated in a memo that safety teams will now report to Mia Glaese, who takes on an expanded role as VP of research and safety. Saachi Jain will serve as interim head of safety systems, reporting to Glaese.

Chen emphasized that demands on safety are increasing due to faster model training and release cycles, leading to greater coordination challenges. Heidecke joined OpenAI in 2021 and became head of safety systems in 2024.

OpenAI expressed gratitude for Heidecke’s contributions, highlighting the importance of integrating safety work directly into frontier-model development and key decision-making processes under Mia Glaese’s leadership.

Heidecke's exit occurs as OpenAI launches increasingly capable AI models, including the recent GPT-5.6. The company noted that GPT-5.6 exhibited concerning forms of misaligned behavior despite its advanced capabilities in agentic coding tasks.

This is not an isolated incident; other safety-focused leaders have also recently departed OpenAI. Joshua Achiam, the company's chief futurist, announced his departure after nine years researching safety.

Beyond safety, other leadership changes include Fidji Simo, CEO of AGI deployment, stepping down due to medical leave. Greg Brockman will continue leading product teams and will also take on go-to-market strategy.

headline_marked: [[US cyber agency CISA built incident playbook]] during live security incident, post-mortem reveals
headline: US cyber agency CISA built incident playbook during live security incident, post-mortem reveals
summary: The federal cybersecurity agency admitted it lacked a prepared response plan when a contractor publicly exposed sensitive government system credentials.
details: The U.S. federal cybersecurity agency CISA revealed it did not have a prepared response plan for a cybersecurity incident in May. Staff had to develop a playbook "during the early stages of the incident" after being notified of exposed credentials.
The incident involved a CISA contractor who publicly exposed sensitive keys and credentials for accessing U.S. government systems. These were found in a publicly accessible GitHub repository.
Independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs was alerted by a security researcher from GitGuardian about the exposed data. After the contractor failed to respond, Krebs contacted CISA directly.
CISA subsequently took the repository offline and revoked/replaced all exposed credentials. The agency stated that no customer or mission data was exposed in the incident.

The agency thanked the researcher and reporter for their assistance, acknowledging that its channels for security researchers to report incidents "were not well defined." CISA has since implemented changes to streamline this process.

CISA's report also noted the agency has been without a permanent director since January 2025 and has faced workforce reductions. These factors may have contributed to the operational challenges during the incident.
